bel-downtown-park.name: Bellevue Downtown Park
bel-downtown-park.blurb: A 20-acre circle of lawn ringed by a half-mile promenade and a stepped canal ending in a 240-ft-wide waterfall, with the Bellevue skyline rising behind.

spawn.note: NE Gateway plaza (NE 4th × Bellevue Way) by the Piloti sculpture looking SW over the canal toward the waterfall.

extent.description: Whole park: circular promenade, canal ring, waterfall + reflecting pool (south-west), central 10-acre meadow with the WWI memorial elms, NE Gateway plaza with Piloti (2023), Inspiration Playground (SW), formal gardens; Old Main Street is one block south.
extent.edges: Bellevue Square (north), Bellevue Way (east), Main St (south), 100th Ave NE (west).
extent.vertical: Mostly flat; waterfall drop ~3 m into the pond (estimate).

structures.name: Canal + promenade ring
structures.form: Half-mile circular gravel/concrete promenade lined with memorial benches and shade trees on one side and a stepped, shallow concrete canal on the other; completed as a full circle in June 2017.

structures.name: Waterfall and reflecting pond
structures.form: 240-ft-wide sheet waterfall over a stepped stone/concrete edge into a reflecting pond — the canal's terminus.

structures.name: Piloti (Marc Fornes / THEVERYMANY, 2023)
structures.form: White perforated aluminium shell canopy on fluted column-legs at the NE Gateway plaza (NE 4th × Bellevue Way); water feature (2021) beside it.

plaques.title: A park by competition
plaques.text: An international design competition (67 entries) picked Beckley-Myers' circular promenade, canal and waterfall in 1984; the park opened in 1987.

plaques.title: 240-ft waterfall
plaques.text: The half-mile promenade ends at a 240-ft-wide waterfall that falls into a reflecting pond.

plaques.title: Remembering WWI
plaques.text: The central elms are a 1926 memorial to Eastside World War I veterans, restored from 2015.

plaques.title: Piloti
plaques.text: Marc Fornes' 23-ft Piloti (2023) is made of 6,000 white aluminium panels held by 180,000 rivets.

interaction.primary: Walk the half-mile loop (timer + step counter achievement); toss a coin into the reflecting pond.

iconic.frame: Waterfall and pond in front, Bellevue towers rising behind the trees

seasonal: Autumn leaf colour on the promenade ring

lines.text: Morning! Lovely loop today.
Once around the promenade is half a mile.
The waterfall's 240 feet wide — loudest spot in the park.
Rainier's out over the trees today.
Ducks are thrilled.

The design won an international competition in 1984 — a circle of lawn, a canal and a waterfall.
Those elms in the middle are a 1926 memorial to local WWI veterans.
Lunch walk between meetings.
Best place to think through a bug.
Take a photo with the waterfall!
The park is so peaceful.
Such a big park in the city centre.

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
